name: Haitian Creole
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand sources agree (1 agree, 0 refine), none contradicts
catalog_quote: Normal, automatic on the last syllable of each word ... The automatic stress on the last syllable of the word is maintained in connected discourse, thus serving as a marker of word-boundaries
sweep_summary: Haitian Creole (hait1244) is in the catalog as fixed-strict final stress on Hall 1953:24 sec. 1.71, quote verified verbatim at djvu lines 1426-1432; note this search of works with stress in the title target's catalog_cite field is blank although this catalog record carries the locator 'Hall 1953:24 §1.71'). The four title-hits reduce to two works. (1) Brousseau 2003 'The accentual system of Haitian Creole' (Plag ed., pp. 123-146) is the one dedicated study of Haitian word accent and the highest-priority unread source; it is closed everywhere checked (OpenAlex closed/no repository fulltext, Semantic Scholar CLOSED, De Gruyter paywalled and bot-gated, HathiTrust search-only, Google Books no preview, archive.org none); Glottolog lists it three times (424151, a misspelled 181896, and 684549 misattributed to editor Plag). (2) Cadely 1997 'Prosodie et cliticisation en créole haïtien' (Études Créoles 20(1)) was already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 run and was read: p. 83 states, as a premise shared by creolists, that the last syllable of the word or rhythmic group bears the tonic accent, with five examples, and pp. 83-84 show enclitics cannot bear the accent ([mandél] not *[mandelí]) — this refines (word vs rhythmic group; clitic extrametricality) but does not contradict the classification. The APiCS survey chapter (Fattier 2013, held by the project) independently states 'fixed word stress on the last syllable of the word' (confirms). WALS has no 14A/15A value for Haitian Creole (hcr). No new first-hand statement supersedes Hall 1953; best new statement read is Cadely 1997:83 (refines, does not supersede).g. Cadely 1986 'Le système accentuel du créole haïtien', Valdman 2015 ch. 2) were not completed.

new_statements.quote: nous acceptons sans discussion l'idée que semblent partager un grand nombre de créolistes, à savoir que c'est la dernière syllabe du mot ou du groupe rythmique qui porte l'accent tonique en CH. Voici en (11) le profil accentuel des mots en CH : (11) marasá « jumeaux » lestomák « estomac » respekté « respecter » machín « voiture » batimán « bateau »
new_statements.translation: we accept without discussion the idea that a great many creolists seem to share, namely that it is the last syllable of the word or of the rhythmic group that bears the tonic accent in Haitian Creole. Here in (11) is the accentual profile of words in HC: marasá 'twins', lestomák 'stomach', respekté 'to respect', machín 'car', batimán 'boat'
new_statements.citation: Cadely, Jean-Robert Joseph. 1997. Prosodie et cliticisation en créole haïtien. Études Créoles 20(1): 77-88. DOI 10.3406/ecreo.1997.1578
new_statements.reading: Fixed word-final stress, agreeing with the catalog's fixed-strict final coding; the added nuance is that the accent domain is 'the word or the rhythmic group' and that reduced enclitic pronouns/particles are inherently unaccented, so the host's final syllable keeps the accent ([mandél], not *[mandelí]). The statement is a first-hand phonologist's characterization with examples, but it is presented as a premise taken over from other creolists, not as a new finding.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation (Hall 1953:24, sec. 1.71) is present verbatim in the held archive.org scanned text and at the corresponding page of the HathiTrust PDF we hold (PDF p. 29 = printed p. 24); locator and content are correct. (2) Deciding source: a 1953 primary descriptive grammar (AAA Memoir 74) — authoritative but old; it is not the most detailed source on Haitian accent (Brousseau 2003 is), and a 2015 reference grammar (Valdman) exists; neither is. Glottolog's top 'grammar' entries (Fattier 1998 atlas, Lefebvre 1998, Glaude 2013, DLI/Valdman courses) are syntax-, lexicon- or pedagogy-oriented and not better stress sources than Hall. no JIPA Illustration of Haitian Creole exists in Crossref (only Férère's 1970s-80s segmental notes). (3) Two open sources download

sources.citation: Hall, Robert A. Jr. 1953. Haitian Creole: Grammar, Texts, Vocabulary (American Anthropological Association Memoir 74), p. 24 (sections 1.7-1.71, continuing onto p. 25) — read via archive.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: "1.7. Stress is of two types: 1.71. Normal, automatic on the last syllable of each word: e.g. /sɔti/ 'go out' [so'ti]; /kɔplotaj/ 'plot' [kõplo'taj]; etc. (cf. examples given passim in 1.1). The automatic stress on the last syllable of the word is maintained in connected discourse, thus serving as a marker of word-boundaries, indicated in our phonemic transcription and in conventional spelling by a space: e.g. /jo vini vwé mwé/ 'they came to see me'." sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Pour les fins de cette présentation, nous acceptons sans discussion l'idée que semblent partager un grand nombre de créolistes, à savoir que c'est la dernière syllabe du mot ou du groupe rythmique qui porte l'accent tonique en CH. Voici en (11) le profil accentuel des mots en CH : (11) marasá « jumeaux » lestomák « estomac » respekté « respecter » machín « voiture » batimán « bateau » [...] pour que tout se tienne, il faut que l'accent tonique tombe sur la dernière syllabe, en l'occurrence sur le pronom /li/, de telle sorte que l'on puisse prononcer *[mandelí]. Cette pronunciation est inacceptable [...] la forme employée par tous les locuteurs du CH est [mandél].
sources.locator: p. 83, section III (third argument), examples (11)-(12); continuation p. 84
sources.note: English: 'For the purposes of this presentation we accept without discussion the idea that a great many creolists seem to share, namely that it is the last syllable of the word or of the rhythmic group that bears the tonic accent in Haitian Creole. Here in (11) is the accentual profile of words in HC: marasá twins, lestomák stomach, respekté respect, machín car, batimán boat. [..] for everything to hold together the tonic accent would have to fall on the last syllable, i.e. on the pronoun /li/, giving *[mandelí].
